nodes.label: On-call engineer
nodes.summary: Receives notifications, looks at dashboards and queries to diagnose.

nodes.label: Monitored services and exporters
nodes.summary: Expose or send numeric measurements (counters, gauges, latency distributions) with labels.

nodes.label: Notification channels
nodes.summary: Email, PagerDuty, OpsGenie and similar receivers.

nodes.label: Collectors
nodes.summary: Scrape targets over HTTP (Prometheus pull model, with a push gateway for short-lived jobs) or receive pushed data (Monarch ingestion routers), enforce label rules and route each series to its shard.

nodes.label: Time series database (region A)
nodes.summary: In-memory recent window with a log, periodic compressed blocks and an index, sharded across hosts. Gorilla holds 26 hours; Prometheus keeps two-hour blocks.

nodes.label: In-memory recent data
nodes.summary: Compressed recent points (delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR values: 16 bytes to 1.37 bytes). 85% of queries in the predecessor system were for the last 26 hours.

nodes.label: Log
nodes.summary: Append-only log of recent data. Gorilla buffers up to 64 kB so a crash can lose a second or two for higher write availability; Prometheus uses a write-ahead log to protect the in-memory block.

nodes.label: Compressed blocks on disk
nodes.summary: Every two hours the compressed block is written to disk with a checkpoint marker; Prometheus blocks hold chunks, index and metadata.

nodes.label: Series index
nodes.summary: Maps metric names and labels to series. Each new label combination is a new series, so high-cardinality labels inflate it.

nodes.label: Shard manager
nodes.summary: Paxos-based system that assigns shards to nodes and redistributes them when a node fails; write clients buffer one minute of data meanwhile.

nodes.label: Replica in another region
nodes.summary: Each series is written to two hosts in separate regions with no consistency guarantee; reads fail over to the other region.

nodes.label: Long-term store (rollups)
nodes.summary: Persistent store for history. In Gorilla the in-memory database is a write-through cache of an HBase store; with Thanos, immutable blocks are uploaded to object storage and the compactor downsamples and applies retention. Combining them is our design.

nodes.label: Rule evaluators
nodes.summary: Periodically run alerting and recording rules (standing queries in Monarch); an alert is pending until its condition has held for the configured time, then firing. Run in the same zone as the data.

nodes.label: Alertmanager
nodes.summary: Deduplicates, groups, routes, silences and inhibits alerts; can run as a cluster.

nodes.label: Query API and dashboards
nodes.summary: Ad hoc queries and graphs, served from the closest healthy replica.

nodes.label: Alternative: independent meta-monitoring
nodes.summary: A separate, simpler system watches the monitor and a dead man's switch alert fires if alerts stop arriving. Industry practice, not from the sources.

edges.label: persist history (write-through in Gorilla, block upload in Thanos)

steps.caption: A collector scrapes a target (or receives pushed data).
It finds which node owns the series.
The point is written to the in-memory block.
A second copy is streamed to the other region without a consistency guarantee.
It is appended to the log for recovery.
Every two hours the compressed block is flushed to disk.

flows.name: A rule fires and someone is paged

steps.caption: The evaluator runs the alert expression against the local data.
After the condition has held for the configured time the alert fires and goes to Alertmanager.
Alertmanager groups it with similar alerts and sends one notification.
They open dashboards and query to diagnose.
Writes to the failed node's shards are buffered by the clients for about a minute, dropping older points.
The shard manager reassigns the shards to other nodes, usually within thirty seconds.
If the move is too slow, reads can be pointed at the other region.
Reads fail over to the other region's copy.
Writes continue to the surviving region; the failed region's reads stay off until it has been healthy for the retention window (26 hours in Gorilla).
A service starts adding a user ID to a label, creating a new series per user.
The index and memory grow with every new series; without per-tenant series limits (our design reasoning) the shard can run out of memory.
